title: Ask an expert

fn.en: Talk about experts and high achievers; ask well-formed questions.

gr: question forms in every tense, and subject questions

can.en: I can ask a well-formed question in any tense, including questions about the subject.

acts.say: Say which two words you would want on your own reference.

cols.en: 🤝 About how somebody is with people

items.r: somebody who reaches an unusually high level in what they do
not willing to let anything stop you
having special training or knowledge for a job
a senior manager in a company
somebody whose job is to study a subject in detail
the way you think and feel about something

items.s: Her only ___ at nineteen was to get out of the town she was born in.
He has received various ___ for his work with young people.
She uses her ___ to raise money for a children’s charity.
Which ___ of the job did you like least?
You mustn’t ___ him — nobody could have known.
I find it hard to ___ when there is music on.

items.q: She is enormously ___ — she has been in three orchestras since she was twelve.
He is far too ___ of everybody else’s work and not enough of his own.
She works on a ___ youth education programme.
Nobody can say she is not ___ — she has never once given up.
The company has a reputation for ___ thinking.
What ___ you to apply in the first place?

sub.en: Watch what happens when the question word IS the subject.

items.q: Who ___ you to play the piano?
items.why: When the question word is the subject, there is no auxiliary and no inversion: Who taught you?

items.q: And who ___ you teach the piano to?
items.why: Here who is the object, so the ordinary auxiliary + subject + verb order returns.

items.q: What ___ you to apply for the job?
How long ___ you been working here?
What ___ you doing when they called?
___ you use to work at the Almaty branch?
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 19: the question takes did + use to.

items.q: What ___ it like to work there?
Which of these questions is correct?
o: What do you think motivates people?
What do you think does motivate people?
items.why: After do you think, the word order goes back to a statement: … motivates people, not … does motivate.

rows: ___|no auxiliary — the word order does not change
___|be moves in front of the subject

items.sit: You are interviewing somebody and you want the reason behind their choice.
o: What made you apply for this job?
What did make you apply for this job?
What you made apply for this job?

o: How long have you been doing this?

How long do you do this?

o: Who did teach you to play?
Who did you taught to play?

items.sit: You want to know what the experience of the job feels like.
o: What’s it like to work there?

items.sit: You want their opinion on what drives high achievers.
o: What do you think motivates them?

items.sit: You want to know about a job they had years ago.
o: Did you use to work in television?
Do you use to work in television?

lines.s: So — what ___ you go into research?
An anthropologist came to my school when I was fifteen.
I never found out her name. That still annoys me.
How long ___ you been doing it now?
Slower than people imagine. Mostly reading.
Did you ___ to work in a lab?
For two years. I was terrible at it.
And what do you ___ makes a good researcher?

write.q: Write eight questions you would ask somebody you admire in your field. Include at least one subject question (Who…? What…?), one present perfect question, one past question, one question with used to, and one with “do you think”.
plan: what they think about the field now
write.model:
1. What made you choose this field in the first place?
2. Who taught you the most in your first two years?
3. How long have you been doing it now?
4. What’s it like on an ordinary Tuesday, rather than in an interview?
5. Did you use to think you would be doing something else?
6. What was the hardest year, and why?
7. What do you think separates the people who stay from the people who leave?
8. Who would you ask this question to, if you could ask anybody?

speak.q: Ask five of your questions out loud, then answer three of them about yourself and your own work or studies.
speak.model: What made you choose this field? Who taught you the most in the first two years? How long have you been doing it? What’s it like on an ordinary Tuesday? What do you think separates the people who stay from the people who leave? — For me: I chose it because somebody let me try it once. I’ve been doing it for six years. And what separates people, I think, is whether they can be wrong without taking it personally.
